# Enterprise limiter fixtures

`enterprise-8.1.json` contains synthetic Redis records generated by the licensed
Sidekiq Enterprise 8.1.0 limiter API, using a disposable local Redis service and
UTC. It contains data only; no commercial implementation code is included.

The generator loaded the existing local Sidekiq and Pro packages, Enterprise
scripting support, and the Enterprise limiter subsystem. The full Enterprise
entrypoint was unnecessary and required an unavailable `gserver` dependency.
No gems were installed.

The scenario created a concurrent limiter with two slots, completed three
acquisitions, and captured its state while a fourth acquisition held one slot.
It invoked four bucket limiters three times each, one for each supported interval;
two window limiters twice each, using a symbolic and a numeric interval; a leaky
limiter twice successfully and once over limit; and a points limiter with a
200-point estimate corrected to 150, followed by an over-limit attempt.
The concurrent acquisition was released after capture.

Additional scenarios captured actual concurrent waiting, overtime, and reclaimed
locks with a short lock timeout, then a waiting acquisition with a longer timeout.
Separate leaky and points limiters each exhausted a one-second allowance and
waited for the next permitted acquisition, recording wait duration in seconds.

These records establish key names, data types, persisted configuration, metric
units, optional metrics, and retained counters. Tests replay the records at their
captured observation time. Additional synthetic edge cases cover metrics absent
from this short runtime scenario, malformed values, expiration, and scanning.

The opt-in integration tests replay these data in dedicated disposable services:

```sh
LAZYKIQ_TEST_LIMITER_REDIS=redis://127.0.0.1:17389/1 \
LAZYKIQ_TEST_LIMITER_CLUSTER=redis://127.0.0.1:17400 \
  go test ./internal/sidekiq -run TestLimiterLiveRedis -v -count=1
```

The cluster service must have at least three primaries. These tests write and
remove fixture keys, so the supplied connections must never point to production.
They verify all five types, every bucket history resolution, distributed discovery,
and unchanged key counts, serialized values, and non-increasing TTLs during reads.
